# Welcome {.unnumbered}

Welcome to the learning line Quantitative Methods to Understand E&BI. Across
three courses, you learn how to turn questions about entrepreneurship,
organisations, markets, and innovation into quantitative evidence that you
can defend. This learning line helps you to understand the research papers used in other
courses, to write a quantitative thesis, and to analyse data carefully at
work.

The learning line is about more than formulas and R commands. You learn to
read and produce evidence with care: to choose a method, explain its logic,
interpret its output correctly, and recognise what the available data cannot
show.

## Why this matters if you want to start a business

Founders make decisions all the time: which product, which price, which customers,
how much to ask from an investor. Each of these decisions gets better with
evidence. Today the evidence is easy to get. You have your own sales data, a
quick survey, and R or an AI assistant that turns data into numbers within
seconds.

The numbers are the easy part. The hard part is to know what a number tells
you, when to trust it, and what to do next. An AI assistant will give you an
average, a p-value, or a regression table, together with a confident
sentence. Sometimes the sentence is wrong. This learning line gives you what
you need to read such output yourself, to verify and check it, and to turn
it into a decision.

Every lecture starts from a practical question, tries to answer it with
data, and then introduces the theory that is needed to interpret the results
of the analysis. The theory helps you
understand what R or an AI assistant is telling you. The same skills help you
during your studies: in your venture projects, when you read research in
other courses, and in your thesis.

The three courses form one connected line. QM Intermediate and QM Advanced
build on the concepts introduced in QM Basic.

By the end of the learning line, you should be able to:

- translate an E&BI question into variables, comparisons, and testable claims,
- work reproducibly with data in R and communicate what the output means,
- conduct high-quality data analysis for work and research,
- evaluate the strength and limits of evidence in research papers,
- design and complete a quantitative thesis.

## How to use this book

The permanent menu on the left is organised into QM Basic,
QM Intermediate, QM Advanced, and Supplementary resources. On a
small (mobile) screen, open the menu with the button at the top of the page.
The book is made for a laptop or a tablet. On a phone, wide formulas and
tables need sideways scrolling.

Within each course, follow the chapters in order:

- **Lecture chapters** introduce a question and a dataset. They teach you how
  to analyse the data in R, together with the theory you need to interpret and
  understand the output.
- **Tutorial chapters** help you recall, combine, and apply what you have
  learned. They give you guided practice and prepare you for the exam.
- **Course exam resources** include a cumulative formula sheet for QM Basic,
  a code sheet for QM Intermediate, and a mock exam at
  the end of each of those courses.
- **Supplementary resources** contain general help with R and mathematics, and the [How to succeed in this course](resources/how-to-succeed.qmd)
  page with printable weekly checklists.

### How a lecture chapter is organised

Every lecture chapter has the same three parts.

- **Before class.** A short preparation, usually a video, a warm-up task,
  and one prediction.
- **Lecture material.** The full material of the lecture: the question, the
  data, the R code, the theory, and worked examples. In the lecture we cover
  the most important parts and leave time for questions and for trying the
  methods yourself. The text has every step, so you can read it again and re-watch the videos
  at your own pace.
- **After class.** Practice with model answers. The first step is always to
  read the lecture material once in full. Then come recall questions and
  tasks.

Some boxes (coloured blocks of text) appear in many chapters:

- **Definition** boxes hold the core terms.
- **Optional** boxes are grey and closed until you click on them. They hold
  formal versions, derivations, and side topics for students who want to
  learn more. They are not part of the exam.
- **Try it** boxes ask you to attempt a step before you open the answer.
- **A founder's decision** shows how the method of the lecture helps to make
  one decision in an invented venture (always an invented example).
- **What ... can and cannot ...** boxes have titles such as "What a
  correlation can and cannot say" or "What a residual check can and cannot
  show". They give the limits of a result and say what you can still do
  with it.
- **Check the AI** shows an answer from an AI assistant that contains errors.
  You find them and write the corrected answer.
- **Steps for a complete answer** boxes show what a complete written answer
  contains, for example the five steps of a test. The mock exams ask for the
  same steps.

Always do the preparation marked "Before class" before you come to the
lecture. The [How to succeed](resources/how-to-succeed.qmd) page shows what a
week can look like for proper preparation and successful learning in the course.

## Lecture preparation and external videos

Most "Before class" sections include a "Video preparation" box.
Watch the videos listed there before the lecture and write short notes on
the concepts that the box names. When a box gives a start and an end time,
watch only that part. QM Basic uses videos from MIT OpenCourseWare,
jbstatistics and Brandon Foltz. QM Intermediate uses Brandon Foltz's
Statistics 101 series. Under some lists, a collapsed note shows where the
videos differ from this book. The theory sections in the
lecture material also link to external explanations. You can watch them again
after a lecture, or when you missed a lecture.
External sources may use different notation or cover more material than this
course. Follow the notation and scope stated in this textbook.

## R and main dataset

You will work with R throughout all three courses. You already met R in
[Programming for E&BI](https://walshc.github.io/ebi-prog/). If you have
forgotten a command or workflow, use the [R Refresher](resources/r-refresher.qmd)
and the earlier course as references.

Our shared dataset records pitches shown on the US television programme
*Shark Tank*. In a televised pitch, entrepreneurs present a venture or
product to a panel of investors known as sharks. The entrepreneurs may ask
for money in exchange for an ownership share. The investors question them,
negotiate, and may announce a deal during the episode.

Most chapters use one file with 19 variables. Download it directly here:
[shark_tank_teaching.csv](data/shark_tank_teaching.csv). You do not need an
account or any other website. The file is a teaching version of Satya
Thirumani's [Shark Tank US Dataset](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/thirumani/shark-tank-us-dataset),
which is the original source of the data.
One row represents one recorded televised pitch. The file contains 1,441
pitches from completed Seasons 1 to 16. The variables include identifiers for
the pitch and the episode, the industry of the venture, a short written
description, and the amount and equity that the entrepreneurs first asked
for. They also record whether a deal was announced on air and the terms of
that deal. Last, they record the gender of the people who presented, in broad
groups that the source of the data defined.
Examples and tasks that use the Shark Tank file carry this tag: [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag}.

## Tutorials and assessment

QM Basic and QM Intermediate end with an exam with open questions, which
counts for 100% of the grade. QM Basic ends with a written exam. In QM
Intermediate, you take the exam in TestVision, the university's system for
computer exams, and R is available during the exam. Tutorials in all courses prepare you for
the exam.

Go directly to the [QM Basic Formula Sheet](basic/formula-sheet.qmd),
[QM Basic Mock Exam](basic/mock-exam.qmd),
[QM Intermediate Code Sheet](intermediate/code-sheet.qmd), or
[QM Intermediate Mock Exam](intermediate/mock-exam.qmd) when you prepare for
the exam.

## Working with AI

Each course has its own AI assistant, a Tilly bot. You find the link on the
course overview pages of [QM Basic](basic/overview.qmd) and
[QM Intermediate](intermediate/overview.qmd).

When you use AI, follow four steps, Attempt, Ask, Verify, Explain:

1. Attempt to solve the question yourself and identify where you are stuck.
2. Ask the AI for a hint, a counterexample, or a question that helps you find
   your mistake. Be precise and detailed when you write a prompt for the AI.
   A precise prompt gets a better answer.
3. Verify the response against the data, course notation, and R output.
   Checking the answer is the key skill when you work with AI.
4. Explain the result in your own words, so that you really understand it.
   Ask the AI for feedback on this explanation, or bring it as a question to a lecture, a
   tutorial, or your classmates.
